analysis.one_liner: Cuts federal student aid to colleges whose degrees do not qualify graduates for required professional licenses.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, so no federal student aid program was ever conditioned on programs actually qualifying graduates for licensure.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made colleges ineligible for federal student aid — including GI Bill education benefits, Pell grants, and workforce grants — for any program meant to prepare students for a licensed job (like nursing, teaching, or cosmetology) unless completing the program actually qualifies the graduate to sit for the license exam in their state, and unless the school arranges required clinical placements or internships. Schools would have had to sign an executive-level certification that each of their career programs is accredited and meets licensure prerequisites, and would have had to warn students in writing — with a signed, handwritten acknowledgement — before enrolling them in a program that does not meet the license requirements where they live. It also would have required online schools to be legally authorized in every state where their students live. It was referred to three House committees and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Students — and especially veterans using GI Bill benefits, which the bill covers alongside Pell grants and workforce grants — would gain protection against paying federal-aid dollars for degrees that leave them unqualified to take the licensing exam for the job they trained for. States and legitimate accredited programs would also gain by cutting out competitors that advertise into states where their credentials are worthless.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students and veterans using federal aid

how_it_helps.text: An institution would lose federal student aid eligibility for any licensure-prep program unless completing it fully qualifies the student to take the required entry exam and be licensed or certified in the student's own state and any state the school advertises into [S2] [S3].

Schools would have to arrange timely clinical placements, internships, or apprenticeships for the academically related pre-licensure requirements, a step some students currently must fend for themselves on [S2] [S3].

The bill covers federal aid across the Higher Education Act, WIOA workforce grants, adult education funds, GI Bill programs under title 38, and military education benefits under title 10, closing the gap where bad programs simply switch funding streams [S3].
Online and correspondence programs would have to be legally authorized in every state where enrolled students live, with states able to take and publicize student complaints [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Colleges — chiefly for-profit career colleges and large online providers — offering licensure-prep programs that are not accredited or do not meet state licensure prerequisites would lose access to federal student aid for those programs. Compliant institutions would bear the cost of the new executive-level certification, timely placement of clinicals and internships, and multistate authorization.

drawbacks.text: The compliance demands are heavy for small schools: an executive certification for every gainful employment program, updates within 10 days of any change, a three-year waiting period to reestablish eligibility, and guaranteed clinical placements the school may not control — costs that could push marginal programs offline even where some students benefit from them [S3].

The bill's own notice provision lets a school enroll a student in a program that does not meet licensure requirements in the student's state, as long as the student signs a handwritten acknowledgement — a waiver that could shift blame for a worthless credential onto the student [S3].

Requiring programs to qualify graduates in the student's own metropolitan area and state could push schools to drop low-volume licensure tracks where exam or placement routes are scarce, reducing options for rural students.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection is sound and cheap for students: a degree that does not qualify you to take the license exam for your field is not worth tuition, and the bill attacks that problem at its source by conditioning federal aid. The heavier burdens fall on schools, some compliance rules (10-day certification updates, guaranteed placements) are blunt, and the handwritten-acknowledgement waiver is a genuine loophole. On balance, the protection to students and veterans outweighs the compliance cost, but the bill as drafted would have needed refinement in committee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees, then to a subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi introduced the bill on March 21, 2023, and it was referred to the Education and Workforce, Armed Services, and Veterans' Affairs committees.
On April 11, 2023, the House referral to Veterans' Affairs was sent to the Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity, and no further action appears in the record.
No other member of the House cosponsored the bill, and it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Colleges — especially for-profit and online institutions — offering licensure-preparation programs that are not accredited or do not meet state licensure prerequisites are better off, because they keep full access to federal student aid, including GI Bill dollars, without the certification, placement, and state-authorization conditions the bill would have imposed. Students enrolled in such programs are in the same position as before: the federal money keeps flowing regardless of whether the credential works in their state.

for.name: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made the case for conditioning federal aid on programs qualifying graduates for licensure.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the 118th Congress, leaving it to die in committee.

against.name: House Veterans' Affairs Committee leadership
against.role: Referring committee; Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity
against.what_they_did: The referral went to the Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity and no subcommittee or full-committee action followed for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Armed Services Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so it never drew enough support from either side to reach a vote and no roll-call shows how the parties would have split.

industries.note: These schools dominate the segment of the market offering licensure-prep programs that are not accredited or do not satisfy state licensure prerequisites. The bill would have cut off federal aid — including GI Bill funds — to those programs, ending a revenue stream built partly on degrees that do not work in the student's home state.

Online schools would have to be legally authorized in every state where their students live and meet programmatic accreditation in those states, adding cost — but reciprocity agreements would let compliant providers keep multi-state reach. The bill's notice rule also targets the common online-school practice of enrolling students in programs that do not qualify them for licensure where they live.

industries.industry: Community colleges and accredited nonprofit programs
industries.note: Most established programs already meet accreditation and licensure prerequisites, so the main costs are certification paperwork and guaranteed clinical placements. The bill would help them by removing federally funded competitors whose credentials do not work.
